prisoner.name: Thad Coffin
prisoner.description: Thad Coffin was jailed following anti-nuclear civil disobedience at a General Electric plant producing B-1 bomber engines in Evandale, Ohio. After a May 15, 1984 trespass arrest, Coffin was convicted May 28 and sentenced June 5 to thirty days in jail. A contemporary report describes a fast during confinement and release at a special hearing on June 22.
prisoner.body: Source: Nuclear Resister26, August2,1984, PDF2. Earlier arrests are not assumed continuous with the June sentence custody.

case.charges: May15,1984 trespass at General Electric B-1 bomber engine plant, Evandale, Ohio.
case.sentence: Thirty-day jail sentence imposed June5; refused cooperation and was carried to jail on a stretcher. Report says he fainted in the visiting room June21 and was released at a special hearing the next day, with unsupervised probation until September1. Thirty days is sentence, not actual time served. Earlier April17/May1984 arrests are not counted as continuous admission. Source: https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NR026_19840802small.pdf#page=2

expected_prisoner.name: Ernest Bromley
expected_prisoner.description: Ernest Bromley was an American minister, Quaker and civil rights and peace activist. A founding member of the Freedom Riders, he played an active role in protests of racial segregation in the Southern United States. He also organized rallies in Cincinnati which protested the Vietnam War and segregation. Bromley was also a pioneer of the modern American tax resistance movement. In 1942 he refused to display a "defense tax stamp" on his car. He redirected the $7.09 cost of the stamp that would have gone to the war effort and gave it instead to Methodist overseas relief. He was jailed for 60 days and lost his position as minister. He produced and edited a local newsletter called Peacemaker for many years. Peacemakers was the name of an organization that he and his wife Marion helped found that encouraged pacifism and resistance to war taxes and the draft. Peacemakers developed a fund for families of people imprisoned for acts of conscience. He also worked to desegregate Coney Island and the University of Cincinnati College Conservatory of Music. In the 1970s, the Internal Revenue Service tried and failed to seize the Bromley home for non-payment of taxes. In 1977 the War Resisters League gave the Bromleys its annual Peace Award. At 78, he was arrested again in 1991 for attempting to scale the White House fence in protest of the war in the Persian Gulf. He passed away in 1997 due to complications from cancer, remembered for his contributions to the anti-war movement.

case.charges: 1984 General Electric Evandale anti-nuclear trespass prosecution and failure to cooperate with court proceedings.
case.sentence: Initial April17,1984 GE protest arrest followed by release. After failure to attend May2trial, warrant issued and later re-arrest brought actual jail admission on 1984-05-13. Trial May16 resulted in seven-day sentence with time-served credit. Actual release 1984-05-17 explicitly reported. Seven is imposed term/credit, not an asserted actual7day total. Source: https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NR026_19840802small.pdf#page=2

expected_prisoner.name: Maurice McCrackin
expected_prisoner.description: The Rev. Maurice McCrackin was a Cincinnati minister who for ten years refused to pay federal income taxes because he would not 'buy guns or bombs.' In 1958 federal agents carried him bodily before a commissioner; indicted in November, he was jailed for an indefinite contempt term, went on a hunger strike, and on Dec. 12 was convicted of refusing an IRS summons and sentenced to six months and a $250 fine.

expected_cases.charges: Refusing an IRS summons; contempt of court (war-tax resistance)
expected_cases.sentence: Initial September 12, 1958 arrest followed by release; not counted as continuous confinement. Actual county-jail admission November 24, 1958 documented in National Guardian, December 15, 1958, p. 4: https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/national-guardian/1958-12-15-11-9-nat-guardian.pdf. Six-month sentence and $250 fine imposed December 12, 1958; actual parole May 29, 1959 confirmed in National Guardian, June 15, 1959, p. 5: https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/national-guardian/1959-06-15-11-35-nat-guardian.pdf. September arrest and release documented in National Guardian, September 29, 1958: https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/national-guardian/1958-09-29-10-50-nat-guardian.pdf. Later accounts of Christmas Eve sentence service or January 31 Allenwood arrival are not the first county-jail admission. Existing six-month duration override retained; precise aggregate service remains unresolved.
